short: The preeminent German fighter of 1917, central to the heavy Allied losses of "Bloody April".
full:
Reaching frontline German squadrons in December 1916, the Albatros D.III was a heavily armed, streamlined fighter that reclaimed air superiority for the Central Powers. Borrowing the sesquiplane wing layout from French Nieuport designs, it combined exceptional agility with the substantial firepower of twin synchronized Spandau machine guns. Its robust, plywood-skinned semi-monocoque fuselage set a new standard for aerodynamic efficiency and structural strength.

The type was the principal weapon of the Luftstreitkräfte during "Bloody April" in 1917, a month in which the Royal Flying Corps suffered devastating casualties. Flown by elite units such as Manfred von Richthofen’s "Flying Circus," the D.III decimated Allied bomber formations and obsolete fighters. Although plagued by early structural failures in its lower wing, it remained a formidable opponent throughout 1917 and continued in operational service until the end of the war, ultimately being retired by postwar operators in 1923.
